questions.problems: The stem's 'as reported in the passage' lets A and B be struck because the passage says the subgroups did not differ in age or nightly sleep, and C is never reported, so the item reduces to locating the 86% vs 74% sentence rather than reasoning about confounds.
C stacks two errors (posterior pituitary and adrenal medulla), so it is easy to drop.
C (same percentage) is weak because the passage gives 73 vs 69 directly; the question is mostly number lookup.

questions.ambiguity: B: a student could argue that unequal store access follows from residential segregation by income, though segregation describes where groups live, not the uneven spread of resources.

questions.problems: D is an overreach no careful reader would pick.
C is factually false (self-rated health predicts later illness and mortality) and A is implausible for n = 2,400, so only B and D are real contenders.

questions.ambiguity: C: placing stores where expected sales are highest sounds like a cost-benefit (rational choice/exchange) idea, but the 'system running efficiently as a whole' clause points to functionalism.
B: she explains her own negative outcome by external causes, which is also self-serving bias; the 'contrast between her two explanations' favours actor-observer, but this is a known gray zone.

questions.problems: A, B and C are all negative or cognitive symptoms, so anyone who knows that positive symptoms differ from the rest can pick D without knowing the dopamine pathway.

questions.ambiguity: B: teacher expectations shaping a student is the textbook Pygmalion setup, but the stem asks about her self-concept formed from how others seem to see her, not about her performance.

questions.problems: A and B contradict the stem's own facts (falling death rate, high birth rate), so the item is close to a giveaway.

questions.ambiguity: A: students often confuse role strain with role conflict, but the demands come from two different roles (resident and parent), which makes it role conflict.

overall: The two passages read like real MCAT P/S experimental and survey passages, and their numbers are internally consistent: the subgroup means average to the table values (nap 78, stress 64) and the Quartile 1 car split gives 31%. The strongest items are P1-3, P2-3, P2-5 and P2-6, which need real data reasoning, and S3, S5 and S8, which test the right fine distinctions. The weakest parts are distractors that the stem or passage rules out at once (P1-2's 'as reported' plus the explicit no-difference sentence, S7's A and B, P2-3's C, S4's single-category tell). Several passage questions (P1-6, P2-2) are table lookups and will feel easier than real MCAT items. Overall the set skews EASY; it needs two or three harder reasoning items per passage to match real exam difficulty.
